<reason>Both sides were competent and the clash narrowed cleanly to a single question: should a high unit price be an independent veto, or merely a term to bargain over? PRO held a coherent line (permission is not obligation; judge total public cost against clinical protection; CON never established that an equivalent cheaper deal is available) and landed a genuine dilemma in closing on CON's "revisit the terms" fallback. But CON did more of the decisive work. It reframed the motion's operative clause into a testable question ("what does the high price buy?"), exploited PRO's own repairs — central purchase, free release to hospitals, capped exposure — to argue that every fix PRO offered neutralises the very feature it asks us to permit, and drove the cap/volume tradeoff into a patient-level harm (rent = courses not bought, access programmes shrunk). Its error-weighing asymmetry (conditional permission is recoverable; a pre-announced acceptance of high prices anchors every later contract and cannot be un-granted) gave a concrete decision rule that PRO answered only by distinguishing "adequacy" tests from "price" tests. CON also converted PRO's honest concession that its case is "an economic mechanism, not a claim about a verified developer walk-away" into a clean burden problem. CON's weaknesses were real: it never squarely answered PRO's sharpest counter — that a delinked lump sum for a small stewardship-limited market implies a high effective cost per course anyway, so "rent" is asserted rather than shown — and two of its turns were clipped for exceeding the cap, an execution cost. That keeps the margin clear but competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]-[B2.3]/[B4.1]: showing that PRO's own safeguards (central purchase, free bedside release, capped exposure) describe a delinked subscription in which the high unit price does no allocative work, so PRO's remedies concede that the price is the problem. PRO's best counterpunch — that CON's "revisit the terms" either concedes the motion or leaves the gap unfilled — was strong but met with the plausible anchoring/recoverability reply.</best_rebuttal>
